options: \(\lVert x \rVert > 0\) for \(x \ne 0\), \(\lVert c x \rVert = \lvert c \rvert\,\lVert x \rVert\), and the triangle inequality
\(\lVert x+y \rVert = \lVert x \rVert + \lVert y \rVert\) for every pair
\(\lVert x \rVert = 0\) for some \(x \ne 0\)
\(\lVert c x \rVert = c\,\lVert x \rVert\) even when \(c\) is negative
questions.explanation: The axioms are positivity, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality. Equality in the triangle inequality is special, not required for every pair. A nonzero vector in the kernel would break positivity. A negative scalar must come out as its absolute value, or the norm could be negative.

questions.explanation: \(\lvert 3 \rvert + \lvert -4 \rvert = 7\). The 2-norm is 5, and the infinity-norm is 4. Subtracting the coordinates gives \(-1\), which is not a norm.

questions.prompt: In the plane, the unit balls of the 1-norm, the 2-norm, and the infinity-norm are
options: three disks of different radii
a diamond, a disk, and a square
a square, a diamond, and a hyperbola
a single square used for all three
questions.explanation: The 1-norm ball is a diamond with vertices on the axes, the 2-norm ball is the round disk, and the infinity-norm ball is the square aligned with the axes. The same radius does not make those three sets coincide. A hyperbola is unbounded, so it cannot be a unit ball.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 230" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>nested unit balls</title><line x1="28" y1="112" x2="256" y2="112"/><polygon points="256,112 249.6,114.7 249.6,109.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="200" x2="140" y2="28"/><polygon points="140,28 142.7,34.4 137.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="128" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="24" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="72" y="44" width="136" height="136" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="68"/><polygon points="208,112 140,44 72,112 140,180"/><text x="158" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">inf</text><text x="162" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2</text><text x="156" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1</text></svg>

questions.explanation: \(\sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\). The 1-norm is 7, and the infinity-norm is 4. Reporting 25 skips the square root.

questions.prompt: The infinity-norm of a vector is
options: the sum of the absolute values of the coordinates
the square root of the sum of squares
the largest absolute coordinate
the product of the coordinates
questions.explanation: \(\lVert x \rVert_\infty = \max_i \lvert x_i \rvert\). The sum of absolute values is the 1-norm, and the square root of the sum of squares is the 2-norm. A product is not a norm: it vanishes when any coordinate does.

questions.figure_alt: A diamond inside a disk inside a square, centered at the origin.

questions.explanation: The larger absolute coordinate is 4. The 1-norm is 7 and the 2-norm is 5. Averaging the absolute coordinates gives 3.5, which is none of the three norms.

questions.prompt: On a finite-dimensional space, any two norms are equivalent. That means
options: the two norms give the same number on every vector
one of them must be the infinity-norm
their unit balls are identical
each is bounded by a constant times the other, and the constants may depend on the dimension
questions.explanation: Equivalence is a two-sided comparison with constants, not equality. The 1-norm and the infinity-norm differ on \((1,1)\). Their unit balls have different shapes. The constants grow with dimension: \(\lVert x \rVert_1 \le n \lVert x \rVert_\infty\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 230" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>nested unit balls</title><line x1="28" y1="112" x2="256" y2="112"/><polygon points="256,112 249.6,114.7 249.6,109.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="200" x2="140" y2="28"/><polygon points="140,28 142.7,34.4 137.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="128" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="24" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><rect x="72" y="44" width="136" height="136" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><circle cx="140" cy="112" r="68"/><polygon points="208,112 140,44 72,112 140,180"/><text x="158" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">inf</text><text x="162" y="76" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2</text><text x="156" y="100" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1</text></svg>

questions.explanation: Three absolute values of 1 sum to 3. The 2-norm is \(\sqrt{3}\), and the infinity-norm is 1. The comparison \(\lVert x \rVert_1 \le \sqrt{n}\,\lVert x \rVert_2\) holds with equality here, since both sides equal 3.

questions.explanation: \(\sqrt{1+1+0} = \sqrt{2}\). The 1-norm is 2, and the infinity-norm is 1. Squaring the 2-norm gives 2, which is the 1-norm of this particular vector, not the 2-norm.

questions.prompt: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds an inner product by the product of 2-norms. One consequence used to prove the triangle inequality is
options: \(\langle x, y \rangle \le \lVert x \rVert_2\,\lVert y \rVert_2\)
\(\lVert x \rVert_1 = \lVert x \rVert_\infty\) for every \(x\)
every norm comes from an inner product
the infinity-norm fails the triangle inequality
questions.explanation: The inequality \(\langle x, y \rangle \le \lVert x \rVert_2 \lVert y \rVert_2\) turns \(\lVert x+y \rVert_2^2 = \lVert x \rVert_2^2 + \lVert y \rVert_2^2 + 2\langle x,y \rangle\) into a perfect square. The 1-norm and the infinity-norm are not equal in general. The 1-norm does not come from an inner product, and it still satisfies the triangle inequality.

questions.prompt: For \(x = (3,-4)\), the 1-norm is 7 and the infinity-norm is 4. What is \(\lVert x \rVert_1 / \lVert x \rVert_\infty\)?
questions.explanation: \(7/4 = 1.75\). In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the comparison \(\lVert x \rVert_1 \le 2\lVert x \rVert_\infty\) allows a ratio as large as 2, and 1.75 sits under that. The reciprocal \(4/7\) swaps the two norms.

questions.prompt: The open ball of radius \(r\) about \(x\), in a chosen norm, is
options: \(\{y : \lVert y-x \rVert \le r\}\)
\(\{y : \lVert y-x \rVert < r\}\)
\(\{y : \lVert y-x \rVert = r\}\)
a closed half-space
questions.explanation: Open means the inequality is strict, so the sphere itself is left out. The nonstrict inequality is the closed ball. Equality is the sphere. A ball of a norm is not a half-space, except in the trivial sense that both are convex.
